 1          Plaintiff Keith Bujold (“Plaintiff”), on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated

 2   whose cash in accounts custodied by defendant Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC dba Wells

 3   Fargo Advisors (“WFA”), a wholly-owned subsidiary of its control person, defendant Wells Fargo

 4   & Company (“Wells Fargo”) (together “Defendants”), was subject to the Wells Fargo Advisors’

 5   Cash Sweep Program, alleges as follows against Defendants, based on personal knowledge as

 6   to Plaintiff and his own acts, and otherwise on information and belief, based on the

 7   investigations of his counsel, which included a review of documents created and distributed

 8   by Defendants, SEC filings, and other publicly available commentary, analysis, and

 9   information. Upon information and belief, Plaintiff believes that discovery will further

10   support the allegations in this class action complaint.

11                                        I.     INTRODUCTION

12          1.      This case arises out of a cash sweep program implemented by WFA, whereby

13   uninvested cash balances in a customer’s account are automatically “swept” and transferred by

14   WFA into interest-bearing bank accounts discretionarily selected by WFA (the “Bank Deposit

15   Sweep Programs,” or “Programs,” consisting primarily of the “Standard Bank Deposit Sweep”

16   and “Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep”) or, in some instances, other sweep arrangements made

17   available to WFA customers. This action concerns only the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs and

18   not any other sweep arrangements.

19          2.      Pursuant to the terms of the Programs, customer cash is swept into accounts held

20   with banks both affiliated with WFA (“Affiliated Banks”), and not affiliated with WFA

21   (“Unaffiliated Banks”) (together the “Program Banks”). WFA implemented the Bank Sweep

22   Programs ostensibly to offer its customers a vehicle to hold cash that offers FDIC insurance on

23   those cash deposits.

24          3.      Upon opening an account with WFA, customers were automatically enrolled in the

25   Bank Sweep Programs, and upon enrollment in the Programs such customers were unable to select

26   any bank deposit cash sweep options which might have offered better terms than those made

27   available by WFA.

28                                                        1                  CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                Case No.
                  Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 3 of 25




 1          4.      While claiming to have designed, implemented and operated the Bank Sweep

 2   Programs as its customers’ agent, in reality, WFA used the Bank Sweep Programs to generate

 3   enormous fees for itself at the expense of its customers who receive only a minimal return on their

 4   cash deposits, while WFA keeps for itself the vast majority of interest and fees the Program Banks

 5   paid out on the cash deposited by WFA’s customers with those Banks.

 6          5.      In its agreement with its customers, WFA specifically acknowledges that it is a

 7   fiduciary vis-a-vis its customers for purposes of the Programs, as the agreements state that WFA

 8   purports to act as its customers’ “agent” not only as when making deposits of customer money

 9   into the Program banks, but also, crucially, when establishing and maintaining the Bank Deposit

10   Sweep Programs. WFA’s actions in designing, implementing, and operating the Bank Deposit

11   Sweep Programs to benefit itself at the expense of its customers constitutes a breach of the

12   fiduciary duties that WFA owes to its customers, the members of the proposed Class here including

13   the Plaintiff, and constitute a breach of the contract that WFA entered into with those customers.

14   Furthermore, WFA utilizes material misrepresentations and the omission of key facts concerning

15   its Bank Deposit Sweep Programs to obscure from its customers how the Programs truly operate.

16          6.      Over the past several months, WFA’s conduct has finally begun to draw regulatory

17   scrutiny. In November 2023, WFA disclosed an investigation by the SEC concerning its Bank

18   Sweep Programs for certain types of accounts. Then in July 2024, WFA announced that it will be

19   changing the pricing of its Bank Sweep Programs to pay customers a higher rate of interest.

20   According to WFA, the price changes will likely cost Defendants an estimated $350 million in

21   yearly revenue, evidence of the massive windfall the Programs provide to Defendants at the

22   expense of WFA’s customers.

23          7.      Plaintiff brings this action individually and on behalf of a Class of similarly situated

24   individuals for breach of fiduciary duty, gross negligence, negligent misrepresentations, breach of

25   contract, and unjust enrichment to recover damages arising out of WFA’s violations of the law,

26   and for such other relief as the Court may deem just and proper.

27

28                                                          2                   CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                   Case No.
                   Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 4 of 25




 1                                   II.     JURISDICTION AND VENUE

 2           8.      This Court has original jurisdiction over the subject matter of this action under 28

 3   U.S.C. §1332(d)(2), as this action is brought as a class action on behalf of class members, one or

 4   more members of the class are citizens of a state different than the Defendants, and the amount in

 5   controversy exceeds five million dollars ($5,000,000), exclusive of interest and costs.

 6           9.      The Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendants because Wells Fargo, WFA’s

 7   parent company and control person, has it principal place of business and is headquartered in this

 8   District, regularly transacts business in California, and thus has minimum contacts in California

 9   and in this District.

10           10.     Venue is proper under 28 U.S.C. § 1391 because among other things, defendant

11   Wells Fargo maintains its headquarters in this District, defendant WFA has offices in this District,

12   and a substantial part of the events, omissions, and/or relevant conduct by Defendant giving rise

13   to Plaintiff’s claims occurred in this District.

14                                               III.   PARTIES

15           A.      Plaintiff

16           11.     Keith Bujold (“Plaintiff), is a customer of WFA and a resident of New Mexico.

17   Plaintiff has been a customer of WFA since at least 2014 and opened accounts with WFA in which

18   cash was held in varying amounts over the course of the life of the accounts. At all relevant times,

19   the cash held in Plaintiff’s accounts was automatically “swept” into low-interest bearing bank

20   accounts pursuant to the Programs – accounts for which WFA ultimately received fees and returns

21   on investments far higher than what was paid out to Plaintiff.

22           B.      Defendants

23           12.     Defendant Wells Fargo is a financial services company headquartered in this

24   District at 420 Montgomery Street, San Francisco, California 94101. Wells Fargo describes itself

25   as a leading financial services company that provides a diversified set of banking, investment and

26   mortgage products and services, as well as consumer and commercial finance through banking

27   locations and offices, the internet and other distribution channels to individuals, businesses, and

28                                                         3                  CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                 Case No.
                  Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 5 of 25




 1   institutions in all 50 states, the District of Columbia and in countries outside the U.S. Wells Fargo

 2   is named as a defendant herein in its capacity as the parent company and control person of Wells

 3   Fargo Clearing Services, LLC, dba Wells Fargo Advisors.

 4          13.     Defendant Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC dba Wells Fargo Advisors is a

 5   dually registered broker-dealer and Registered Investment Advisor or “RIA” that offers brokerage

 6   and investment advisory services to its nationwide client base. Wells Fargo Advisors is a trade

 7   name used by Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC. Defendant offers brokerage services to

 8   Plaintiff and members of the proposed Class, acting as its customers’ agent regarding the

 9   establishment, maintenance, and operation of the Programs. Wells Fargo Clearing Services, LLC

10   dba WFA is a majority-owned subsidiary of defendant Wells Fargo. In its BrokerCheck reports

11   filed with the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (“FINRA”), Wells Fargo Clearing Services

12   states that it is 75% or more owned by Wells Fargo, and that as owner, Wells Fargo directs the

13   management or policies of the firm.

14                                   IV.     FACTUAL BACKGROUND

15          A.      The Bank Deposit Sweep Programs Were Established by WFA for Its Own
                    Benefit, Not That of Its Customers’
16

17          14.     Under the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs, available cash balances in WFA
18   customers’ accounts are automatically swept into interest-bearing accounts at either Affiliated
19   Banks or Unaffiliated Banks.
20          15.     The Bank Deposit Sweep Programs consist of two separate but similar programs:
21   the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep and the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep, all of which are
22   discretionarily selected by WFA.
23          16.     The Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep is the primary option for eligible clients and
24   operates by sweeping customers’ cash balances into interest-bearing deposit accounts at one of
25   five banks (the “Program Banks”). These Program Banks are a collection of both Affiliated and
26

27

28                                                         4                   CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                  Case No.
                 Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 6 of 25




 1   Unaffiliated Banks. Under the Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep, customers are precluded from

 2   excluding the Affiliated Banks as a destination for their cash balances.

 3          17.     Certain customers, specifically those with “Resource” accounts and retirement

 4   accounts in WFA’s discretionary advisory programs, cannot elect the Expanded Bank Deposit

 5   Sweep and are restricted to the Standard Bank Deposit Sweep as their Bank Deposit Sweep

 6   Program.

 7          18.     The Standard Bank Deposit Sweep operates by sweeping customers’ cash balances

 8   into interest-bearing deposit accounts at two or more WFA Affiliated Banks.

 9          19.     Each business day, available cash balances in all eligible customer accounts are

10   swept out of the accounts and into one of the Program Banks, depending on which sweep type the

11   account qualifies for and the capacity of the Banks to accept additional deposits. 1

12          20.     Customers’ account statements indicate their cash sweep balance and show interest

13   or dividends which reflect their returns from the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs.

14          21.     WFA, acting as its customers’ “agent”, according to the terms of its contracts with

15   its customers, was legally and duty bound to establish and maintain the Bank Deposit Sweep

16   Programs in the best interests of its customers, not itself.

17          22.     The contractual terms and conditions of WFA’s relationship with its customers,

18   including regarding the Cash Sweep Program, are governed and controlled by the General Account

19   Agreement and Disclosure Document (the “Account Agreement”), and the Wells Fargo Advisors’

20   Cash Sweep Program Disclosure Statement (the “Cash Sweep Program Disclosure Statement”).

21   As explained by the Account Agreement, “the Cash Sweep Program is described more fully in the

22   Cash Sweep Program Disclosure Statement which is included with this Agreement.”

23          23.     The Cash Sweep Program Disclosure Statement defines the relationship between

24   WFA and its customers regarding the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs as follows:

25
     1
26     Certain commercial and public fund account types are ineligible for either Bank Deposit Sweep
     Program and are instead placed in a taxable money market fund. Those accounts are not a subject
27   of the present action and are excluded from the Class.
28                                                           5                  CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                   Case No.
                Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 7 of 25




            Wells Fargo Advisors will act as your agent in establishing and maintaining the
 1          Bank Deposit Sweep Programs, including making deposits to and withdrawals
 2          from the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs. Your first deposit into the Standard Bank
            Deposit Sweep or Expanded Bank Deposit Sweep will constitute your appointment
 3          of Wells Fargo Advisors as your agent in connection with the Standard Bank
            Deposit Sweep or Expanded Bank Sweep.
 4
     (Emphases supplied).
 5

 6          24.     As its customers’ agent, WFA was legally bound to act in the best interest of those
 7   customers.
 8          25.     Thus, under the express terms of the Cash Sweep Program Disclosure Statement,
 9   WFA, acting as its customers’ agent in connection with establishing and maintaining, and
10   thereafter operating, the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs, was duty bound to establish, maintain,
11   and operate the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs in the best interests of its principals, i.e., its
12   customers such as Plaintiff and the members of the proposed Class.
13          26.     Notwithstanding, WFA established, maintained, and operated the Bank Deposit
14   Sweep Programs for its own best interests, contrary to the interests of its customers/member of the
15   proposed Class here, as set forth in more detail below.
16          27.     WFA’s actions vis-a-vis the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs breached its contract
17   with its customers and the fiduciary duties it owed to those customers.
18          28.     More specifically, the Programs were structured as follows. As the first step, the
19   Affiliated Banks—i.e., banks affiliated with WFA—purportedly “set” the rate of interest that
20   would be paid to its customers under the Programs “in consultation” with WFA. WFA does not
21   “negotiate” on its customers’ behalf to try and obtain the best rates of interest for them; rather, it
22   “consult[s]” with its Affiliated Banks, i.e., that is, it agrees and acquiesces to the rates set by
23   WFA’s affiliates regardless of whether those terms are in its customers’ best interest. Indeed, the
24   rates that WFA sets in consultation with its Affiliated Banks are far below the rates WFA
25   customers could have otherwise earned on their cash in the marketplace.
26

27

28                                                          6                   CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                   Case No.
                  Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 8 of 25




 1          29.     As a second step, WFA uses the artificially low rates it sets with its Affiliated Banks

 2   as a benchmark. It then “directs” the Unaffiliated Banks to pay its customers the same low

 3   benchmark rate WFA set with its Affiliated Banks.

 4          30.     WFA and its Affiliated Banks keep the difference between the artificially low rates

 5   WFA pays to its customers and what the Affiliated Banks actually pay or earn, and WFA keeps

 6   for itself the difference between the artificially low rate WFA pays to its customers and what the

 7   Unaffiliated Banks actually offer and/or pay.

 8          31.     By establishing and maintaining the Programs in this fashion, and thereafter

 9   agreeing with its Affiliated Banks to set an artificially low rate to pay its customers, then using

10   that low rate as a benchmark for what WFA’s customers receive from the Unaffiliated Banks, and

11   keeping the difference for itself, WFA breached its fiduciary duties to its customers as their agent,

12   and also breached its contract with those customers that it would act as their agent, not for its own

13   benefit. WFA’s process created a clear conflict of interest that WFA fails to properly disclose or

14   mitigate.

15          32.     As a result of this self-interested process established and maintained by WFA,

16   WFA’s customers receive the same low rates on their cash balances in their WFA accounts from

17   all Program Banks. Conversely, WFA retains the majority of the returns generated by its

18   customers’ cash balances, in the form of fees it collects for itself from the beneficial payments it

19   receives from the Program Banks for its customers’ cash deposited with those Banks.

20          33.     Moreover, WFA states that it “assumes no obligation to seek or negotiate interest

21   rates in excess of any reasonable rate of interest the Affiliated Banks are willing to credit,” but it

22   omits to disclose that the “reasonable” designation is false and mischaracterizes the interest rates

23   offered by the Affiliated Banks. Indeed, those rates are anything but reasonable and, as stated

24   above, WFA compounds the harm by directing the Unaffiliated Banks to pay WFA’s customers

25   those same, unreasonably low rates that the Affiliated Banks pay.

26          34.     In contrast to the unreasonable returns WFA pays its customers, WFA retains as

27   fees for itself a substantial portion of the beneficial returns on each of its customers’ cash, which

28                                                          7                   CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                   Case No.
                  Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 9 of 25




 1   portion is not disclosed to its customers, and instead is described as an “up to” calculation

 2   applicable in the aggregate to all customer cash deposited with the Program Banks, such that no

 3   individual customer can ascertain WFA’s fees on that customer’s cash sweep.

 4          35.     WFA exercises discretion, in its capacity as the agent of its customer, as to the

 5   Programs and its key features, including designing, establishing and maintaining the Programs,

 6   selecting the Program Banks, agreeing to the rates of return for its customers’ cash, making a

 7   reasonability determination as to the rates paid by its Affiliated Banks, deciding how much its

 8   customers will receive in interest on their cash in the Cash Sweep Programs, and deciding how

 9   much WFA will keep for itself in fees for its role in the Cash Sweep Programs.

10          B.      WFA’s Disclosures to Its Customers Regarding the Bank Deposit Cash Sweep
                    Programs Contained Material Misrepresentations and Omissions.
11

12          36.     WFA made material misrepresentations and omitted material information when

13   describing the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs to its fiduciary customers. Then, in late 2023,

14   following a number of lawsuits filed against WFA’s competitors arising out of those competitors’

15   cash sweep programs, WFA changed some of its disclosures regarding the Programs. 2 While the

16   amended disclosures made in late 2023 were still inadequate and contained material

17   misrepresentations   and   omissions   regarding   the Programs,     the changes     reflect   an

18   acknowledgement by WFA that its prior disclosures surrounding the Bank Deposit Cash Sweep

19   Program were not adequate.

20          37.     For example, in the section titled “Rate of Return,” the 2019–2023 Disclosure

21   Statements stated the following:

22          These rates will vary over time and may be lower than rates available to clients
            making deposits directly with the Program Banks or at other banks.
23
     (Emphasis supplied throughout this section unless otherwise indicated).
24

25

26
     2
       The 2023 changes were carried forward to the 2024 Disclosure Statement and were repeated
27   therein verbatim.
28                                                       8                     CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                  Case No.
                Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 10 of 25




 1          38.     The above statement omitted to disclose that the rates WFA paid its customers were

 2   always lower than the customer could obtain by making deposits directly with the Program Banks

 3   or at other banks.

 4          39.     Then, in late 2023, following lawsuits filed against some of WFA’s competitors,

 5   WFA changed the above disclosure to read:

 6          These rates will vary over time and are typically lower than rates available to clients
            making deposits directly with the Program Banks or at other banks.
 7

 8          40.     The late 2023 amended disclosures continued to include material omissions about
 9   the Programs (“typically” does not mean “always”). Notwithstanding, the change reflects an
10   acknowledgement by WFA that its prior disclosures were inadequate.
11          41.     Similarly, in a section titled “Benefits to Wells Fargo and Others,” the 2019 – 2023
12   Disclosure Statements stated:
13          Higher rates of interest than the rates credited by the Affiliated Banks on Expanded
            Bank Deposit Sweep deposits may be available outside of the Cash Sweep Program.
14

15          42.     The above statement omitted to disclose that the rates credited by the Affiliated
16   Banks on Expanded Deposit Sweep deposits were always lower than the customer could obtain by
17   making deposits outside of the Cash Sweep Programs, as a result of the fact that WFA and the
18   Affiliated Banks retained a substantial part of the credit for themselves.
19          43.     From late 2023 forward, that same section of the Disclosure Statements noted that
20   other cash investment options “typically pay you higher rates of interest,” which remained
21   misleading as “typically” does not mean “always.”
22          44.     Similarly, the 2019–2023 Disclosure Statements represented that:
23
            We and the Program Banks may pay rates of interest on the Expanded Bank Deposit
24          Sweep that are lower than the prevailing market interest rates.

25

26

27

28                                                         9                      CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                     Case No.
                Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 11 of 25




 1          45.       The above statement was misleading in that the rates of interest paid under the

 2   Programs were always significantly lower than prevailing market rates. Moreover, for 2023

 3   forward, the Disclosure Statements made the following revelation:

 4          The Program Banks pay rates of interest on the Bank Deposit Sweep Program
            deposits that are significantly less than the spread those banks earn on deposits.
 5

 6          46.       The Disclosure Statements omitted additional material information. For example,
 7   in its 2019–2023 Disclosure Statements, WFA simply stated “[y]ou may elect not to participate in
 8   the Cash Sweep Program and/or periodically invest cash balances directly in available money
 9   market mutual funds or other products offered as direct investments outside of the Cash Sweep
10   Program,” but failed to disclose to its fiduciary customers – whom it had automatically placed in
11   the Programs – that they would earn a higher rate of return had they chosen other options for their
12   cash balances.
13          47.       Starting with its late 2023 Disclosure Statements, WFA changed the disclosures
14   above to its fiduciary customers to read:
15
            You may elect not to participate in the Cash Sweep Program and/or periodically
16          invest cash balances directly in available money market mutual funds or other
            products offered as direct investments outside of the Cash Sweep Program, options
17          which likely generate a higher rate of interest or yield than the Cash Sweep
            Program.
18
19          48.       In addition, the following material information was entirely omitted from the 2019
20   – 2023 Disclosure Statements:
21          The interest rates paid to client accounts in the Bank Deposit Sweep Program are
            deducted from these payments, and Wells Fargo Advisors retains the remainder.
22
            Accordingly, Wells Fargo Advisors has an incentive to pay lower interest rates to
23          participating accounts. Note that the fee Wells Fargo Advisors receives from the
            Program Banks usually exceeds the interest paid to participating client accounts
24          by a substantial amount. Moreover, due to the contractual arrangements in place
            between the Unaffiliated Banks and Wells Fargo Advisors, the rates paid out to
25          clients will be substantially lower than the Federal Funds Effective Rate and will
26          not increase as quickly as the Federal Funds Effective Rate.

27

28                                                        10                  CLASS ACTION COMPLAINT
                                                                                 Case No.
                Case 3:24-cv-04616-VC Document 1 Filed 07/30/24 Page 12 of 25




 1          49.     Those disclosures, added in late 2023, still omitted material information in that

 2   WFA failed to disclose to each of its fiduciary customers the amount of fees it was keeping for

 3   itself from their beneficial returns paid by the Program Banks on their account balances, and also

 4   failed to disclose that the fees WFA received from the Program Banks always exceeded the interest

 5   paid to participating client accounts by a substantial amount.

 6          50.     Finally, defendant WFA falsely described the rate of return provided to its fiduciary

 7   customers on their cash assets as “reasonable,” when in fact it was not. As a result, WFA’s

 8   fiduciary customers were left entirely uniformed of the spread between the returns generated by

 9   their own cash and the minimal payments they ultimately received on those cash balances and

10   were not in a situation to give informed consent regarding WFA’s Cash Sweep Programs.

11          C.      WFA Breaches Its Contract with Its Customers by Failing to Obtain
                    Reasonable Rates of Interest for Their Cash Assets as Well.
12

13          51.     In its contract with its customers that governs the Cash Sweep Programs, WFA
14   undertook a duty to negotiate “reasonable” rates of return on its customers’ cash balances, and thus
15   it was contractually required to do so.
16          52.     However, the rates agreed to by WFA for its customers were not reasonable. This
17   is because WFA agreed to allow its Affiliated Banks to pay unreasonable rates to WFA’s
18   customers, and then directed the Unaffiliated Banks to pay the same unreasonable rates.
19          53.     Further, despite not possessing an ownership interest in its customers’ beneficial
20   returns on their cash balances deposited with the Program Banks, WFA misused its fiduciary
21   relationship with its customers to retain a substantial portion of those funds for its own benefit.
22          54.     In so doing, WFA breached its contract with its customers related to the Cash
23   Sweep Program.
24                                      V.      Class Action Allegations
25
            55.     Plaintiff re-alleges and incorporates by reference the allegations set forth above.
26

27

 1             56.   Plaintiffs bring this action individually and as a class action pursuant to Rules 23(a),

 2   23(b)(2), and 23(b)(3) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure on behalf of the Class consisting of:

 3   All persons who held cash positions in accounts custodied by WFA, and whose cash was subject

 4   to defendant WFA’s Programs from 2018, until defendant WFA’s unlawful conduct alleged herein

 5   ceases.

 6             57.   Excluded from the Class are governmental entities, institutional and other non-

 7   retail investors; Defendants and any of its affiliates, legal representatives, employs, or officers; the

 8   judicial officer(s) and any judicial staff overseeing this litigation; and counsel for Plaintiff and the

 9   proposed Class, including other attorneys and staff at each respective firm.

10             58.   Plaintiff reserves the right to amend the Class definitions if further investigation

11   and discovery indicates that the Class definition should be narrowed, expanded, or otherwise

12   modified.

13             59.   This action has been brought and may be maintained as a class action under Federal

14   Rule of Civil Procedure 23.

15                                                Numerosity

16                                               Rule 23(a)(1)

17             60.   Class members are so numerous that their individual joinder is impracticable. The
18   precise number of Class members and their identities are unknown to Plaintiff at this time.
19   However, defendant WFA’s wealth management services oversee nearly $1.9 trillion in client
20   assets through the work of approximately 12,000 financial advisors, and Plaintiff believes that the
21   members of the proposed Class number in the thousands. Accordingly, Plaintiff and the Class
22   satisfy the numerosity requirement of Rule 23. Class members may be notified of the pendency of
23   this action by mail, published notice, or other appropriate methods.

 1                Existence and Predominance of Common Questions of Law and Fact

 2                                        Rule 23(a)(2), 23(b)(3)

 3          61.     Common questions of law and fact exist as to all members of the Class and

 4   predominate over questions affecting only individual Class members. These common legal and

 5   factual questions, each of which may also be certified under Rule 23(c)(4), include the following:

 6                  a. Whether defendant WFA owed fiduciary duties to Plaintiff and the putative
                       Class members in connection with the Programs;
 7

 8                  b. Whether defendant WFA breached its duties to Plaintiff and the putative Class
                       members in establishing, maintaining, and/or operating the Programs;
 9
                    c. Whether defendant WFA made material misrepresentations and/or omissions
10                     to Plaintiff and the putative Class members regarding the Programs;
11
                    d. Whether defendant WFA breached its contract with Plaintiff and the putative

13                  e. Whether defendant WFA was unjustly enriched by its wrongful conduct;
14                  f. Whether this case may be maintained as a class action under Fed. R. Civ. P.

                       monetary relief; and

                    h. Whether and to what extent Class members are entitled to attorneys’ fees and

                                                Typicality
20
                                               Rule 23(a)(3)

22          62.     Plaintiff’s claims are typical of the claims of the Class because he was a customer
23   of Defendant that had his cash balances improperly managed by WFA through its administration
24   of the Bank Deposit Sweep Programs. Thus, Plaintiff’s claims are typical of the claims of the
25   members of the Class as the claims arise from the same course of conduct by Defendant, and the
26   relief sought within the Class is common to the members of each.
27

 1                                             Adequacy of Representation

 3          63.       Plaintiff will fairly and adequately protect the interests of Class members. Plaintiff
